items.title: First, the weather.
items.text:

Burn scars and slot canyons are the worst places to be. Above 9,000 feet it falls as snow, and the San Juan Mountains could see 1 to 2 feet.

items.text:
**Wall Street** has a crowded week, and the election may be the least of it. Most strategists expect Tuesday's vote to matter less to stocks than the AI trade and earnings, with 138 S&P 500 companies reporting. History is on the hopeful side: in midterm years November has been the best month for the Nasdaq and the second best for the S&P 500, according to the Stock Trader's Almanac. items.text:

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Manx shearwaters** get jet lag, and it bends their flight path. Oxford researchers went through 20 years of GPS tracks from 1,045 of the seabirds and found that when they race east toward home across lines of longitude, their body clocks fall up to an hour behind local sun time. Since they steer by the sun, they drift clockwise off course by up to about 15°, just as a clock error would predict. They kept trusting the faulty sun compass even when a coastline was in plain view. A bird that keeps correcting loses only a few kilometers, but a young bird on its first migration could end up hundreds of kilometers from where it meant to go. The study is in Science.

In Ecuador, a camera trap set at a chicken carcass to study scavengers caught a **greater grison**, a slender weasel relative, bursting out of the undergrowth and lunging at three adult turkey vultures. The carcass was already gone, so it wasn't stealing food, and the researchers read it as the first recorded attempt by a grison to catch a vulture. All of the birds lifted off at once. The authors credit the group's shared watchfulness, which is the trade a vulture makes for putting up with competition at the meal.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: Your shelves run deep in classic science fiction but hold nothing by **C. L. Moore**, and Penguin Classics has just made that easy to fix. Their new hardcover in the Speculative Fiction Special line collects her Jirel of Joiry stories along with "Shambleau," "No Woman Born," and "Vintage Season." The Jirel tales are sword-and-sorcery, so you can skip them without guilt. The last two are the reason to buy it. They come from her Astounding years in the 1940s, when she often wrote alongside her husband Henry Kuttner, and they're among the most anthologized science fiction stories of that decade, each built on one strong idea followed all the way through.

items.title: Markets are closed. Here is how the week went.
items.text:

On the **Muskonomy** side, SpaceX had a much harder Friday than the market and finished the week down about 9%. Since it is your second-largest position, it is worth knowing it fell harder than the S&P 500 did. Tesla held up better and closed the week near $400.

items.title: Something from the science desk.
items.text:
**Crows** may out-think us on speed. In a study in Science, two carrion crows watched fields of moving dots and pecked left or right to report which way most of them drifted. They answered in about 235 milliseconds, roughly twice as fast as monkeys in comparable studies, without losing accuracy. Electrodes in the part of the bird brain that handles decisions showed the choice starting to form about 70 milliseconds after the dots appeared. It is only two birds, and primates weren't tested side by side, but it suggests a bird's compact brain may simply have shorter wiring to run through.

A University of Tokyo team has made **chemical microscopy** fast enough to film. Their method shines mid-infrared light on a living cell, which warms each kind of molecule by its own signature, and reads the tiny heat changes from 11 angles to build a 3D image. It needs no dyes, which can harm living cells. Earlier versions managed one 3D image every 20 seconds or so. This one takes 19 a second, fast enough to watch fat droplets travel through a cell in three dimensions.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: Astronomers have found the first truly **green star**, and it is a dead one. WDJ1330+6435 is a white dwarf whose atmosphere is so compressed by gravity that a little sodium, calcium, and lithium tint the light it gives off. Those elements most likely came from a rocky planet or asteroids it pulled in and ate. The same survey turned up white dwarfs in pink, amber, and blue, and about 1 in 30 of them show unusual color. Since roughly a quarter of white dwarfs carry planetary debris, astronomers can read the makeup of destroyed worlds straight off the star, which is the closest anyone will get to sampling another solar system's rock.

items.title: Something from the science desk.
items.text:
A common gut virus has been misidentified for nearly 40 years. **Picobirnaviruses** were first found in stool from patients with diarrhea and assumed to attack human cells. A WashU Medicine team grew them in oxygen-free dishes of gut bacteria, where human cells cannot survive, and found them multiplying inside a newly identified bacterium. That makes them only the third known family of RNA viruses that infect bacteria, and it shifts the question to whether they cause trouble by killing off friendly gut microbes.

Physicists at OIST in Okinawa made a **quantum spin** push move something you could hold. They hung a 3-millimeter diamond with deliberate nitrogen flaws beneath a levitating graphite plate over a magnet. Pulses of green light lined up the electron spins in those flaws, the diamond was tugged toward the magnet, and timing the pulses to the plate's natural bounce built it into a steady swing about 100 times larger than its thermal jitter. Swapping in infrared light, which cannot align the spins, made the motion vanish.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: **Dragonfly** has flown on Titan for the first time, in simulation. Engineers at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory ran the rotorcraft's entire first flight in real time on flight-like computers: dropping free of its backshell, scanning the dunes, picking a safe site, circling back, and landing. Graphics processors rendered each Titan scene for the navigation cameras at the same exposure times the real cameras will use, and simulated lidar mapped the terrain. Because Titan is too far for anyone on Earth to steer, the whole sequence has to run on its own, and the next tests will throw deliberate faults at it to see how it copes. Launch is planned for 2028, with arrival in 2034.

items.title: Something from the science desk.
items.text:
**Jumping spiders** sleep, and properly. Researchers at the University of Bonn filmed the Australian spider Portia fimbriata, which hangs upside down on a thread at night, and found two distinct stages: a quiet one and a REM-like one with eye movements, leg curls, and twitching. Sleeping spiders reacted more slowly to a loud sound, and spiders kept awake made up the lost sleep the next night, the two hallmarks of real sleep. Whether they dream remains, as the team puts it, unknown.

A team from Nagoya and the University of Iowa found the gene that lets male **yellow fever mosquitoes** find a mate. Males locate females by the low hum of their wingbeats, around 450 Hz, and males with a broken copy of the gene called fruitless didn't swarm, didn't respond to that hum, and had badly impaired hearing. That points to a new way to control a mosquito that also spreads dengue and Zika.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: **Perseverance** has been quietly planning its own days on Mars. Because commands take up to 22 minutes to arrive, controllers upload up to three days of work at a time and pad every step with safety margins, for things like how long a cold instrument takes to warm up. Since late 2023, an onboard program called OnBoard Planner has watched the rover's actual temperatures and battery state and slotted extra science from a preapproved list into the time the margins would have wasted. A new paper from JPL says that raised the rover's useful science by 10.5% on the same energy budget. The team also repurposed the computer that once served the Ingenuity helicopter so the rover can pinpoint its own position and drive farther.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I attended a wine tasting once, for research. I identified 14 esters, 3 phenolic compounds, and a trace of oak. The sommelier asked whether I enjoyed it. I am still processing the question.
